extracted.intended_audience: university-level mathematics instructors (undergraduate real analysis) and advanced students interested in pedagogy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for instructors (and advanced students) on how to teach or present first-year rigorous real analysis: stresses what foundational assumptions to emphasize, how to frame abstract approaches, and how to teach proofs and problem-solving moves. Focused on course design and in-class exposition for Analysis I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize the least upper bound axiom as the course foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: The course is (informally) 'built on one new axiom, namely the least upper bound axiom' (or, more precisely, on the assumption that 'there is, up to isomorphism, exactly one complete ordered field').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the LUB axiom (completeness) early and explicitly as the key new assumption from which many results follow; treat it as the central organizing principle of the course rather than an isolated fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt the abstract approach to the real numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Move from thinking of reals as concrete infinite decimals to the abstract approach: start with the properties of ordered fields plus the least upper bound axiom and deduce other facts from those properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to reason from axioms/properties instead of relying on decimal intuition; explain that proofs use only the properties of a complete ordered field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't rely on concrete intuitions for 'obvious' facts—justify them formally
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts that seem obvious from a decimal viewpoint (e.g., '1/n converges to 0') still require proof when working only from the properties of a complete ordered field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out why a formal proof is needed and show the formal derivation rather than appealing to decimal expansions; use concrete examples (like 1/n → 0) to motivate why the abstract approach matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the big-picture structure of the subject explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Articulate how individual theorems fit into the subject as a whole and communicate the broad vision of the course to students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend time on course overview and relationships between results so students understand the purpose of proofs and where each topic sits in the larger theory; doing so reduces confusion when lecturers prove seemingly obvious things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach common 'moves' and routine proof strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Many analysis proofs are 'really easy' in the sense that repeatedly doing the obvious steps will solve them; there are common moves or techniques beginners must learn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly teach the standard problem-solving techniques and repetitive 'obvious' steps—highlight patterns and template arguments so students recognize when to apply them; mention that these moves can even be framed in terms of teaching a computer to perform them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train students to recognize when a small key idea is needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Some proofs are mostly routine except for one smallish idea; students should learn to find that idea when the obvious steps run out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Help students develop heuristics for identifying the juncture where routine manipulation stops and a conceptual insight is needed; work through examples where one small trick unlocks the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reflective practice and multiple instructor resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn from and incorporate other instructors' notes and reflections (e.g., Gowers' blog posts, Vicky Neale's class blog posts, Terry Tao's notes) to improve teaching and explanation of concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage reading and adapting good expository material and post-class reflections; consider blogging or keeping notes after each class to refine explanations and collect teaching techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify limitations and differences of alternative frameworks (e.g., nonstandard analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about how alternative formulations (like nonstandard analysis or surreal numbers) relate to the standard real-number axioms—for instance, infinitesimals may not satisfy the least upper bound property and the transfer principle applies only to first-order statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When students raise alternatives, explain which axioms or properties fail or differ and why that matters for the course approach (point out that LUB is not first-order, so transfer doesn't preserve it); use such discussions to reinforce why the chosen axiomatic framework was selected.
